name: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
description:
Adversaries may exploit software vulnerabilities in order to elevate privileges. Exploitation of a software vulnerability occurs when an adversary takes advantage of a programming error in an application, service, within the operating system software, or kernel itself to execute adversary-controlled code. Security constructions, such as permission levels, will often hinder access to information and use of certain techniques. Adversaries will likely need to perform privilege escalation to include use of software exploitation to circumvent those restrictions. 

When initially gaining access to a device, an adversary may be operating within a lower privileged process which will prevent them from accessing certain resources on the system. Vulnerabilities may exist, usually in operating system components and applications running at higher permissions, that can be exploited to gain higher levels of access on the system. This could enable someone to move from unprivileged or user- level permission to root permissions depending on the component that is vulnerable.

telemetry.name: Application Permission
telemetry.description: Declared or granted permissions of a mobile application.
telemetry.collection_focus: Compare manifest declarations with runtime granted state using authorized package inspection and own-app permission checks.

providers.name: Android logcat
providers.scope: Permitted logs from a consented test device/emulator; output depends on build, permissions and instrumentation.

providers.name: Android dumpsys
providers.scope: Point-in-time service/package state on an authorized development device.

providers.name: Instrumented test application
providers.scope: Own-app permission, API and state callbacks; not universal visibility into other apps.

configuration: Use a disposable emulator or owned development device with approved debugging. Record OS/API level, app version and instrumentation privileges.
Collect only relevant logcat buffers/tags and service snapshots; add explicit own-app instrumentation for events absent from OS logs.
Forward sanitized logs and compare before/after state. Remove test data and revoke debugging access after the lab session.

configuration_example.label: Inspect the owned Android lab application
configuration_example.note: Read-only snapshot on a consented debug device. Replace the example package with your owned test app. Output and access vary by Android build; this is not a permission-request event stream.

telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: Android tooling does not imply iOS coverage. Standard mobile apps cannot observe all other apps or protected OS internals; MDM status is not full API, filesystem or content telemetry.
telemetry.anomaly_design: Per owned device, app version and permission state: unexpected API/permission changes, background activity and network destinations. OS privacy restrictions and emulator differences limit observability.

telemetry.name: Host Status
telemetry.description: Host health and availability observations such as heartbeat, shutdown or degraded state.
telemetry.collection_focus: Collect agent heartbeat and OS health independently; record missed polls, last-seen time and monitor health.

providers.name: osquery
providers.scope: Scheduled host-state queries; supported tables and privileges vary by OS. Select a table that actually exposes the required object.

providers.name: Linux Audit plus inventory snapshots
providers.scope: Events explain changes; snapshots describe state at collection time.

configuration: Define the inventory query, allowed host set, interval and least-privileged reader. Store a stable asset ID, observation time and collector version.
Keep successive snapshots and calculate additions, removals and changed attributes. Pair state changes with audit events when available.
Export collector health and missed-poll counts so a missing snapshot is not misclassified as a missing asset.
telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: Snapshots miss short-lived objects and do not identify who caused a change. A generic inventory agent is not guaranteed to expose firmware or kernel-level details.
telemetry.anomaly_design: Compare authorized state snapshots: first-seen drivers/services/modules, unexpected configuration drift and integrity changes. Record collection cadence; absence in a sample is not evidence of deletion.

telemetry.name: Network Traffic Flow
telemetry.description: Connection/flow summaries such as endpoints, duration, byte counts and transport.
telemetry.collection_focus: Collect Zeek conn.log, Suricata flow events or exporter equivalents, including observation point and sampling settings.

providers.name: Zeek
providers.scope: Connection and protocol metadata from traffic visible to the sensor.

providers.name: Suricata EVE
providers.scope: Configured flow, alert, DNS, HTTP, TLS and protocol records.

providers.name: AWS VPC Flow Logs
providers.scope: IP traffic metadata alternative; no packet payload or DNS answer history, and some traffic is not logged.

configuration: Use an authorized lab TAP/SPAN, virtual mirror or gateway interface. Define which traffic crosses it; avoid assuming visibility into every segment.
Enable the required Zeek analyzers or Suricata EVE event types. Export logs with sensor identity, clock synchronization and flow correlation identifiers.
Monitor capture loss, truncation and exporter sampling. Capture payload only with approval and restrictive retention; encryption normally prevents plaintext inspection.
telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: Flows are not packet payloads. NAT, asymmetric routes, encryption, missing mirrors and sampling can hide attribution or content. A destination connection alone does not prove malicious intent.
telemetry.anomaly_design: Per source and observation point: connection rate, destination-host/port fan-out, response/failure ratio and previously unseen destinations. Compare equivalent time windows; separate authorized scanners, NAT and sampling effects.

telemetry.name: OS API Execution
telemetry.description: Instrumented operating-system API calls and their return values.
telemetry.collection_focus: Use an approved EDR trace or instrument the owned lab process at selected APIs. Define API name, caller, sanitized arguments and return status.

providers.name: Application audit logs
providers.scope: First-party service events and request/result fields; schema is application-specific.

providers.name: OpenTelemetry-compatible log pipelines
providers.scope: Transport and normalization of emitted records; do not create missing audit instrumentation.

configuration: Enable the application audit category or instrument the owned lab application at the authorization/action boundary.
Define a schema with timestamp, service, actor, object, action, result and correlation ID. Export structured records through an authenticated collector.
Redact secrets and personal content, separate audit from debug logs, set retention and verify delivery during rotation/restart.
telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: Debug output is not necessarily a durable audit trail. Application developers must emit the relevant event; installing a log pipeline does not make an absent event exist.
telemetry.anomaly_design: Per application, client and route: request rate, rare actions, failure ratios and unusual state transitions. Version changes, retries, health probes and seasonal load need separate baselines.

strategies.name: Detection of Exploitation for Privilege Escalation

analytics.name: Analytic 1758
analytics.guidance: For Android, detect Exploitation for Privilege Escalation by correlating analyst-visible device/network evidence and management state; use streaming or batched telemetry only where the documented collector is deployed. Correlate Application Permission via Android Enterprise DPC / Application Vetting [DevicePolicyManager.getPermissionGrantState(); PackageManager manifest/requested-permission review]; Host Status via Android Enterprise DPC [DevicePolicyManager policy/compliance/security-state queries and SecurityLog events where supported]; Network Traffic Flow via Android Enterprise Network Logging / Enterprise VPN [DevicePolicyManager.retrieveNetworkLogs(): DnsEvent / ConnectEvent; VPN flow metadata]. Alert on a sequence or state change inconsistent with the device/app baseline, approved management policy, or expected user workflow; do not infer unobserved API calls, file/process activity, or payload content from management state alone.

tuning.description: Default 30 days. Align to org patch SLA.
MDM agent, OTA update service, approved Device Admin apps.
Default 600s after root detection. Adjust to MDM check-in interval.

log_sources.name: android:DevicePolicyManager
log_sources.channel: DevicePolicyManager policy/compliance/security-state queries and SecurityLog events where supported

analytics.name: Analytic 1759
analytics.guidance: For iOS, detect Exploitation for Privilege Escalation by correlating analyst-visible device/network evidence and management state; use streaming or batched telemetry only where the documented collector is deployed. Correlate Host Status via Apple MDM [DeviceInformation / SecurityInfo / ProfileList / restrictions and compliance queries]; Network Traffic Flow via Apple Network Extension / Enterprise VPN [NEFilterFlow / per-app VPN / secure-web-gateway flow metadata]; OS API Execution via Application Vetting / Instrumented Dynamic Analysis [Dynamic API/runtime trace: Unified Log entry at level=fault in subsystem com.apple.kernel or com.apple.sandbox within $KernelFaultWindow$ of integrity_check failure — kernel-level fault coincident with integrity failure is the exploit-execution signal; requires super]. Alert on a sequence or state change inconsistent with the device/app baseline, approved management policy, or expected user workflow; do not infer unobserved API calls, file/process activity, or payload content from management state alone.

tuning.description: Default 60s between integrity failure and kernel fault.

log_sources.name: iOS:MDM
log_sources.channel: DeviceInformation / SecurityInfo / ProfileList / restrictions and compliance queries

log_sources.name: iOS:NetworkExtension
log_sources.channel: NEFilterFlow / per-app VPN / secure-web-gateway flow metadata

log_sources.name: mobile:DynamicAnalysis
log_sources.channel: Dynamic API/runtime trace: Unified Log entry at level=fault in subsystem com.apple.kernel or com.apple.sandbox within $KernelFaultWindow$ of integrity_check failure — kernel-level fault coincident with integrity failure is the exploit-execution signal; requires super

software.name: FinFisher
software.description: [FinFisher](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0182) comes packaged with ExynosAbuse, an Android exploit that can gain root privileges.(Citation: Lookout Dark Caracal Jan 2018)

references.description: Blaich, A., et al. (2018, January 18). Dark Caracal: Cyber-espionage at a Global Scale. Retrieved April 11, 2018.

software.name: Pegasus for iOS
software.description: [Pegasus for iOS](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0289) exploits iOS vulnerabilities to escalate privileges.(Citation: Lookout-Pegasus)

references.description: Lookout. (2016). Technical Analysis of Pegasus Spyware. Retrieved December 12, 2016.

software.name: Gooligan
software.description: [Gooligan](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0290) executes Android root exploits.(Citation: Gooligan Citation)

references.description: Check Point Research Team. (2016, November 30). More Than 1 Million Google Accounts Breached by Gooligan. Retrieved December 12, 2016.

software.name: BrainTest
software.description: Some original variants of [BrainTest](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0293) had the capability to automatically root some devices, but that behavior was not observed in later samples.(Citation: Lookout-BrainTest)

references.description: Chris Dehghanpoor. (2016, January 6). Brain Test re-emerges: 13 apps found in Google Play  Read more: Brain Test re-emerges: 13 apps found in Google Play. Retrieved December 21, 2016.

software.name: ShiftyBug
software.description: [ShiftyBug](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0294) is packed with at least eight publicly available exploits that can perform rooting.(Citation: Lookout-Adware)

references.description: Michael Bentley. (2015, November 4). Lookout discovers new trojanized adware; 20K popular apps caught in the crossfire. Retrieved December 21, 2016.

software.name: Pegasus for Android
software.description: [Pegasus for Android](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0316) attempts to exploit well-known Android OS vulnerabilities to escalate privileges.(Citation: Lookout-PegasusAndroid)

references.description: Mike Murray. (2017, April 3). Pegasus for Android: the other side of the story emerges. Retrieved April 16, 2017.

software.name: HummingBad
software.description: [HummingBad](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0322) can exploit unfixed vulnerabilities in older Android versions to root victim phones.(Citation: ArsTechnica-HummingBad)

references.description: Dan Goodin. (2016, July 7). 10 million Android phones infected by all-powerful auto-rooting apps. Retrieved January 24, 2017.

software.name: SpyDealer
software.description: [SpyDealer](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0324) uses the commercial rooting app Baidu Easy Root to gain root privilege and maintain persistence on the victim.(Citation: PaloAlto-SpyDealer)

references.description: Wenjun Hu, Cong Zheng and Zhi Xu. (2017, July 6). SpyDealer: Android Trojan Spying on More Than 40 Apps. Retrieved September 18, 2018.

software.name: Skygofree
software.description: [Skygofree](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0327) has the capability to exploit several known vulnerabilities and escalate privileges.(Citation: Kaspersky-Skygofree)

references.description: Nikita Buchka and Alexey Firsh. (2018, January 16). Skygofree: Following in the footsteps of HackingTeam. Retrieved September 24, 2018.

software.name: Exodus
software.description: [Exodus](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0405) Two attempts to elevate privileges by using a modified version of the DirtyCow exploit.(Citation: SWB Exodus March 2019)

references.description: Security Without Borders. (2019, March 29). Exodus: New Android Spyware Made in Italy. Retrieved November 17, 2024.

software.name: Dvmap
software.description: [Dvmap](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0420) attempts to gain root access by using local exploits.(Citation: SecureList DVMap June 2017)

references.description: R. Unuchek. (2017, June 8). Dvmap: the first Android malware with code injection. Retrieved December 10, 2019.

software.name: Agent Smith
software.description: [Agent Smith](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0440) exploits known OS vulnerabilities, including Janus, to replace legitimate applications with malicious versions.(Citation: CheckPoint Agent Smith)

references.description: A. Hazum, F. He, I. Marom, B. Melnykov, A. Polkovnichenko. (2019, July 10). Agent Smith: A New Species of Mobile Malware. Retrieved May 7, 2020.

software.name: INSOMNIA
software.description: [INSOMNIA](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0463) exploits a WebKit vulnerability to achieve root access on the device.(Citation: Volexity Insomnia)

references.description: A. Case, D. Lassalle, M. Meltzer, S. Koessel, et al.. (2020, April 21). Evil Eye Threat Actor Resurfaces with iOS Exploit and Updated Implant. Retrieved June 2, 2020.

software.name: Zen
software.description: [Zen](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0494) can obtain root access via a rooting trojan in its infection chain.(Citation: Google Security Zen)

references.description: Siewierski, L. (2019, January 11). PHA Family Highlights: Zen and its cousins . Retrieved July 27, 2020.

software.name: DoubleAgent
software.description: [DoubleAgent](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0550) has used exploit tools to gain root, such as TowelRoot.(Citation: Lookout Uyghur Campaign)

references.description: A. Kumar, K. Del Rosso, J. Albrecht, C. Hebeisen. (2020, June 1). Mobile APT Surveillance Campaigns Targeting Uyghurs - A collection of long-running Android tooling connected to a Chinese mAPT actor. Retrieved November 10, 2020.

software.name: AbstractEmu
software.description: [AbstractEmu](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1061) can use rooting exploits to silently give itself permissions or install additional malware.(Citation: lookout_abstractemu_1021)

references.description: P Shunk, K Balaam. (2021, October 28). Rooting Malware Makes a Comeback: Lookout Discovers Global Campaign. Retrieved February 6, 2023.

software.name: Phenakite
software.description: [Phenakite](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1126) has included exploits for jailbreaking infected devices.(Citation: fb_arid_viper)

references.description: Flossman, M., Scott, M. (2021, April). Technical Paper // Taking Action Against Arid Viper. Retrieved November 17, 2024.

software.name: LightSpy
software.description: [LightSpy](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1185) uses the embedded `time_waste` function to bypass standard iOS API restrictions and enable unauthorized audio/video recording. This exploit injects a `.dylib` into the `SpringBoard` process, allowing persistent access to audio and video capture.(Citation: LinkedIn Dmitry LightSpy 2025)(Citation: Threatfabric LightSpy 2024)

references.description: Dmitry Bestuzhev. (2025, April 7). The Coordinated Kill Switch: LightSpy's iOS Destructive Plugin Architecture Manages Device Disablement. Retrieved April 14, 2025.
ThreatFabric. (2024, October 29). LightSpy: Implant for iOS. Retrieved January 30, 2025.
